prize_parts.citation: For the invention and development of the optical lattice clock, in which many neutral atoms confined at the magic wavelength are interrogated free of Doppler, recoil and light shifts, bringing optical clock accuracy and stability to the 1e-18 level

statement.case_for: My preferred configuration is unchanged: the optical lattice clock alone, credited to Katori and Ye. Having read all eight round-1 statements and the chair's questions, I find that the scientific case did not weaken under scrutiny, and the reasons it holds are the ones I would defend without any reference to the count of supporters. The achievement is a bounded invention. The magic-wavelength condition, which removes the differential light shift so that a large ensemble of neutral atoms can be held in a lattice and probed at an optical frequency with Doppler and recoil suppressed, is a distinct idea from a trapped-ion clock and from frequency-comb counting. Its decisive virtue is statistical: many atoms interrogated at once give a stability that a single ion cannot approach, and that is what made systematic uncertainty at the 1e-18 level reachable in practice. Independent laboratories in several countries reproduce it and compare their clocks, so maturity is settled. On the chair's first question, the wording should name the lattice clock itself and its magic-wavelength principle, and should not say precision spectroscopy or optical clocks in general. On the second, I would hold to two names: Katori for the concept and first demonstration, Ye for taking it to extreme accuracy and showing what it can do. On the third, the pending redefinition of the second is a consequence, not a premise. The physics is established now, and a prize does not need to wait for a metrology committee's schedule. I also accept the chair's point that attribution cleanliness is a large part of why most of us land here, and I would say openly that this is partly a judgement about which candidates can be credited fairly, not only which is the greatest science.
statement.case_against: The overlap argument is the real objection and I do not think it is fully answered by saying the lattice is a different idea. A committee could reasonably feel that 1997/2001 (laser cooling and condensates), 2005 (Hall and Hansch, frequency combs and precision spectroscopy) and 2012 (Haroche and Wineland, control of single quantum systems, which led directly to the first optical ion clocks) have already honoured the lineage, and that a clock prize would be a fourth reward in the same family. Second, the most precise ion clocks (Al+) and the early strontium and ytterbium lattice groups are outside the credit, as are the ultrastable-laser developers whose work the 1e-18 numbers rely on; a narrow citation is defensible but it has an attribution cost that I should not wave away. Third, the headline fundamental-physics payoffs, namely dark-matter searches, variation of constants and a redefined second, are still largely prospective. Finally, I work in a neighbouring field, which might make me too ready to see a metrology advance as a discovery.

responses.point: Olsson says the 2005 prize already covers much of the enabling frequency metrology, that Ye's contribution is partly the pushing of accuracy rather than a distinct concept, and that the clock is the safe consensus choice, which is not by itself an argument that it is the best one.
responses.response: I accept that being the consensus choice proves nothing, and I have tried not to lean on it. On substance I disagree with one part. The 2005 prize honoured the frequency comb and Hall's laser stabilisation, which provide the ruler and the ultrastable reference; they do not contain the idea of trapping many neutral atoms at a magic wavelength, and that idea is what changed the signal-to-noise budget. Katori carries the concept. I grant that Ye's role is largely demonstration and extreme performance, but I think that is exactly what the prize tradition rewards in an experimental invention, since 1e-18 was not a foregone conclusion and he showed the systematics could be controlled to that level. Your concern about wording is right and I have moved the citation to name the magic-wavelength lattice explicitly. I also respect your declared willingness to step back from B053 and I think that is the correct handling of the proximity, not a recusal.

responses.point: Eriksson moved to topological insulators (B057) as the only candidate ranked by seven of eight members, with Kane and Mele supplying the Z2 theory and Molenkamp the HgTe experiment, stable after fifteen years of confirmation, while granting that Bernevig, Hughes and Zhang and the 3D contributors are omitted and the 2016 prize overlaps.
responses.response: I agree with you that B057 is the principal rival and that its science is mature, and I keep it as my first alternative. I do not agree that breadth of ranking is the decisive consideration, because seven members placing it somewhere is partly a sign that nobody finds a way to put it first. The omitted HgTe proposers are not a footnote: the Bernevig-Hughes-Zhang proposal is what told Molenkamp's group what to grow and measure, and any three-name credit has to drop either them, the 3D work or one of your trio. A citation built on the Z2 classification and the observation of the quantum spin Hall state could be written, and if the committee settles on it I would not call it unreasonable, but with the 2016 prize close by it leaves more open questions than a two-name clock credit. I would also add that I cannot judge the electronic-structure side as you can, so I give your view on its maturity considerable weight.

responses.point: Mehlig moved from flocking to the lattice clock, noting that the reasons given are independent, that the many-body operation of the clock is itself a statistical-physics result, and asking whether the unredefined SI second argues for waiting or for acting now.
responses.response: Your point about the many-atom operation is one I would have made myself and it is the heart of why the lattice differs from a single-ion clock, so I am glad to see it from a statistical-physics side. On timing, my answer to your question is to act now. The redefinition is a decision by the metrology community that will draw on exactly the comparisons already done between laboratories; waiting for it would make the prize depend on a downstream administrative step instead of on the measured performance. I also share your reservation about overlap with the 2005 and 2012 prizes and I think it is legitimate to keep stating it, which is why the citation should be tight.

responses.point: Pearce, as chair, moved from IceCube to the clock, stating that the clock's largest scientific payoffs are still mostly prospective and that IceCube opens a new observational window more convincingly, while accepting the clock has the cleanest attribution.
responses.response: I take your distinction between an invention and a new window on the universe seriously, and I think it is fair that the clock is the more incremental conceptual step on that axis. Where I differ is on whether the payoffs are prospective: centimetre-scale gravitational time dilation has been measured with these clocks, and clock comparisons already constrain variation of constants and some dark-matter couplings, so some of the reach is realised even though the redefinition and the geodesy are not. Your remark about the IceCube credit is what keeps me away from B041, since two names for a very large collaboration with an AMANDA predecessor is a contest I do not think we can settle among ourselves, and I do not feel I can judge it as an astroparticle specialist.

uncertainties: Whether the committee reads the 2005 and 2012 prizes as sufficient overlap to make a lattice-clock prize redundant; I judge not, but I cannot rule out a reasonable colleague judging otherwise.

Whether leaving out Al+ ion-clock pioneers, early strontium and ytterbium lattice groups and the ultrastable-laser developers will be read as unfair; the three-name limit and the narrow citation are my answer, but this is a real cost.

Whether B057 could be given a citation that survives the omission of Bernevig, Hughes and Zhang; I lack the expertise to judge the solid-state priority history and defer to the condensed-matter members.
I recall the clock performance numbers, the time-dilation measurements and the priority history from memory and have not checked them against sources at this stage.
statement.conflict_note: No change from round 1. I work in atomic physics and laser spectroscopy, a neighbouring field to B027, and my profile documents no collaboration with Katori or Ye. My documented connections (Svanberg, Aldén, Hall's laboratory, Lund colleagues, WACQT and Deep Light Vision) are not with any shortlisted candidate, but my doctoral stay in John Hall's laboratory is professionally adjacent to the 2005 frequency-metrology lineage that the overlap question concerns, and I report it so that colleagues can weigh it. I do not think this requires recusal.
